claims.claim: The game engine has bugs and quirks that remain permanent since updates stopped.

citations.review_text:
Prison Architect is one of those games that's dangerously good at making time disappear. You sit down thinking you'll fix a few cell blocks, optimize a couple work programs, and before you know it it's 2 AM and you're redesigning an entire maximum-security wing because one inmate stole a spoon.

Even after nearly 50 hours, it's still incredibly satisfying watching a prison grow from a dirt lot into a fully functioning (and occasionally completely dysfunctional) correctional facility. The management, planning, and constant problem-solving create that perfect "just one more thing" gameplay loop.

The game is nearly 11 years old at this point, and it definitely shows in places. There are bugs, odd behaviors, and plenty of quirks that longtime players have learned to live with. Since the game isn't receiving updates anymore, those quirks are pretty much permanent fixtures now. Honestly, after all these years, they're less bugs and more part of the Prison Architect experience.

Despite that, the core gameplay still holds up remarkably well. Whether you're building an efficient rehabilitation-focused prison or accidentally creating a powder keg waiting for the next riot, there's always something demanding your attention. Every problem feels like it leads to three more, and somehow that's exactly what makes it so addictive.

If you enjoy management and simulation games, this is still an easy recommendation. Just be warned: it's the kind of game where you look at the clock, think you've been playing for 20 minutes, and discover you've actually lost three hours.

$30 for a ten-year-old game that's not getting ANY updates any more with most of the good new content from said updates being locked behind 13 paid DLCs is biblical levels of greed. I don't care if it's a sandbox game and there's limitless possibilities or whatever, don't buy this at full price. Even if it is a pretty good game.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe staff members and workers getting stuck or stopping work due to bugs.

citations.review_text:
This used to be a really great management game, then Paradox got their hands on it. Now, you need several mods to fix game breaking issues, and even with them installed you still run into bugs that are, at best, tedious to work around. 

Guards occasionally get stuck/bugged and must be fired (extra annoying when you have to fire tazer trained guards). Staff needs/staff rooms are finicky at best. Sprites will break and become partially or completely invisible. Borderless windowed mode makes the game crash on startup about half the time for me. So on and so forth. Mods help alleviate some of the issues, but I still noticed my guards bugging out at times, and there's a laundry list of other problems that I never experienced when Introversion was at the helm. 

If you can get everything working how it's meant to, this might still be a fun prison management sim. It sure used to be, at least. It'll take a lot of trial error regarding which mods and settings are now required, though.

Prison Architect was once a genuinely fun and addictive game. Unfortunately, Paradox Interactive took over after its original release and has since treated it like many of its other titles: squeeze as much money as possible out of the player base through an endless stream of DLCs while leaving serious bugs unfixed.

Anyone familiar with Paradox's business model knows exactly what that means. Players get milked like cows, with content split into countless paid expansions—sometimes for additions as laughably small as different uniform colors. Meanwhile, the actual game becomes increasingly unstable.

One particularly infuriating bug regularly causes employees to get stuck in the staff room while holding food trays near the serving tables. They simply stand there indefinitely instead of eating, resting, or returning to work. Once enough staff members get stuck, essential parts of the prison stop functioning properly. The result is a management game in which your prison can collapse not because of poor planning, but because the staff AI is completely broken.

There is no reliable permanent fix. You can move furniture, rebuild rooms, change layouts, remove serving tables, or create separate staff canteens, but these are temporary workarounds at best. The bug eventually returns. A game that depends entirely on working pathfinding, staff behavior, and resource management becomes borderline unplayable when employees repeatedly freeze while carrying food trays.

I previously said that Prison Architect itself was still worth playing despite Paradox's increasingly obvious cash-grab business model. At this point, I can no longer recommend it. A good game has been buried under DLCs, technical problems, and bugs that should have been fixed long ago.

So thank you, Paradox, for taking a good game and making it practically unplayable. But hey, at least you managed to release a pile of DLCs and charge players for every tiny addition while the basic game mechanics continue to break.

Great game, minor bugs but you can work around them and most fix themselves. Keep in mind there are a lot of mechanics to the game and can get annoying, also many of the features and items are locked in the DLCs. So buy everything if you can you wont regret it, especially if you like city builder games. 

You can change the game settings when you make a new prison, just go to Extras tab in the in game menu to change the game and mutator settings to test them out. A little almost invisible tab on the escape menu on the bottom left turns the game 3D. 

Only real downside to this game is having to google or youtube how to do things frequently because the tutorial leaves a lot of things out. But that goes for any game that has depth. Everything else just takes experience playing around with to get them to work properly. After playing 170 hours I can confidently say all the negative reviews are surly from people who didnt have the time to learn how to play the game or didnt want to buy the DLCs to get the games full potential. To each their own.
